analysis.one_liner: Boosts Social Security cost-of-living raises for seniors and phases out the cap on earnings taxed for Social Security.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have lifted the cap on wages taxed for Social Security and given seniors a faster cost-of-living adjustment, drew 13 Democratic cosponsors but never received a hearing or vote in the House before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how Social Security keeps up with prices by creating a consumer price index for people 62 and older and using it for the annual cost-of-living adjustment. It would also raise more money for Social Security by phasing out the cap on wages subject to the Social Security payroll tax — about $128,400 in 2018 — so that higher earnings would be taxed, with a small matching increase in benefits for those earners.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries, especially older retirees, would gain a cost-of-living adjustment built around the spending patterns of people 62 and older, which typically rises faster than the index used now [S2][S3]. The program's financing would be strengthened by ending the cap on taxed earnings, reducing pressure for future benefit cuts [S2]. Retirees' higher benefits could not be counted as income in ways that cut their SSI or Medicaid benefits [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Current and future Social Security retirees

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish a Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers tracking the spending of people 62 and older, and switches Social Security's annual cost-of-living adjustment to that index, since seniors' costs (notably medical care) tend to rise faster than the index now used for workers [S2][S3].

Phases out the cap on compensation subject to Social Security tax — $128,400 in 2018 — over six years, so that after 2023 all earnings are taxed, bringing in more revenue to the program that pays current and future benefits [S2][S3].
Counts earnings above the old cap in the benefit formula at modest rates, so people who pay the new tax get at least some additional benefit credit for it [S2][S3].
Specifies that any benefit increase from the new index could not be treated as income in ways that would reduce a recipient's SSI or Medicaid benefits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers and self-employed people earning above the wage cap — about $128,400 in 2018 — would pay Social Security payroll tax on a growing share of their earnings above that cap (86% taxed in 2018, shrinking to zero untaxed by 2024) [S2][S3]. Higher earners would also see small benefit increases from the new surplus-earnings formula, but the added tax would far exceed them [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill raises taxes directly on workers and self-employed people earning over the cap, and because employers match the employee share, businesses with highly paid staff face higher payroll costs too — a cost that critics argue can be passed back as lower wages [S2][S3].
The new benefit formula gives higher earners additional benefits for their newly taxed earnings, which offsets some of the new revenue the bill would otherwise devote to the program's solvency [S3].

Switching the cost-of-living adjustment to an elderly-focused index would raise benefits faster than the current formula, increasing program outlays year after year; an honest supporter has to acknowledge this makes the bill's net effect on program finances depend on how large the new tax base turns out to be [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but concentrated on one group: seniors, whose cost-of-living adjustments would better track their actual expenses, particularly medical costs. The costs fall on a much smaller, much higher-earning group — people making over roughly $128,400 — who would see the Social Security tax apply to all their earnings after 2023, though they would receive small added benefit credits in return. The main design weakness is that the bill's new spending (faster benefit growth) and new revenue (the lifted cap) pull against each other, and the bill does not say which wins; scoring the net effect would require the actuarial estimates the record does not include. On balance it is a transfer toward retirees funded by high earners.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees from the day it was introduced and died there when the Congress ended, with no hearing or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 19, 2017 with six original cosponsors and referred the same day to three committees: Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, and Energy and Commerce [S1][S3][S5].
Thirteen House Democrats had signed on as cosponsors, and no Republicans did [S4].
No committee held a hearing or markup, the House never debated the bill, and the Senate never received it; it expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of raising the Social Security payroll tax cap, including high earners who would have paid more, are better off because the bill never advanced; the Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, avoided the issue entirely.

for.name: Rep. Theodore E. Deutch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled initial cosponsors

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: House Ways and Means Committee, chaired by Rep. Kevin Brady (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 19, 2017 and never held a markup or vote on the bill

against.name: Speaker Paul Ryan
against.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the House floor only for referral to three committees, none of which acted on it

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 13 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the bill stayed in committee without a hearing or vote.

industries.note: The bill phases out the cap on wages and self-employment income subject to the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax, so households and businesses at the top of the earnings scale would pay more each year, reaching the full tax on all earnings after 2023.

industries.industry: Government statistical agencies (Bureau of Labor Statistics)
industries.note: The bill appropriates funds for the Bureau of Labor Statistics to build and publish a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, and its higher cost-of-living formula would feed into federal retirement benefit payments.
